passage: Acids and bases are chemical substances that behave differently in nature. While we often associate acids with dangerous liquids, many acids exist in solid forms, such as citric acid found in lemons or oxalic acid in spinach. Similarly, bases are not always harmless; strong bases like sodium hydroxide are highly corrosive and can cause severe skin burns, despite their soapy feel. When an acid reacts with a base, a process called neutralisation occurs. This reaction produces a new substance known as a salt, along with water and heat. It is a common mistake to think that the term 'salt' only refers to the common table salt we use in cooking. In chemistry, a salt is any compound formed from the neutralisation reaction, and these salts can be acidic, basic, or neutral depending on the strength of the reacting substances. During neutralisation, the acid and base do not disappear; their chemical properties are simply modified to form new products. Furthermore, the resulting solution does not always have a pH of exactly 7. If a strong acid reacts with a weak base, the resulting salt solution will be acidic, showing a pH value lower than 7. Understanding these properties helps us identify substances correctly without relying on simple color changes alone.

Every compound that tastes salty is a salt
Every salt must be neutral in solution
Only kitchen salt is made by neutralisation

They vanish and leave only water
